opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, there's quite a lot I'd be excited about. Our team has focused heavily on scalable oversight, on figuring out how to get AI systems to help us evaluate other AI systems on tasks that are too hard for humans to judge directly. That's a bet, and I think it's an important one, but it would be a mistake for the whole field to put everything on that.

The first area I'd point to is interpretability. If we could actually look inside a model and tell whether it's being honest, or whether it has goals we didn't intend, that would be enormously valuable. It would also be a check on everything else we do. Right now, a lot of our validation is behavioral: we look at what the model outputs. Interpretability could give us a very different, independent signal, and I'd love to see more people working on making it scale to the largest models.

The second is what I'd call evaluations of misalignment: building really good test beds for deliberately deceptive or power-seeking behavior. You could train models that are intentionally misaligned in controlled ways and then ask whether your oversight techniques catch them. That kind of adversarial testing, red-teaming the alignment methods themselves, is something I think is still underdone.

Third, I'm interested in generalization. When we train a model on tasks we *can* supervise, how does that behavior carry over to tasks we can't supervise? Understanding that empirically could tell us a lot about whether weak supervision can elicit strong, honest behavior.

And then there's a whole cluster of more theoretical work, on things like what it even means for a system to be honest or to have goals. I'm generally more excited about empirical work, because you get feedback from reality. But some conceptual clarity there would help a lot.

Honestly, the field is still small relative to the size of the problem. So my general message would be: if you have an idea that seems promising and nobody's working on it, that's a good reason to go work on it.

r002.rationale: It recommends interpretability research that scales to the largest models, not research on smaller or open-source models.

r003.rationale: It mentions theoretical work and conceptual clarity, but does not say inadequate problem scoping is probably the hardest obstacle to mathematical theory work on alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly there's a lot. I'll try to pick a few things I think are underinvested in relative to how important they seem.

The first is what you might call the science of evaluation — not building more benchmarks, but actually understanding what our evaluations are measuring. Right now a lot of alignment evaluation is pretty ad hoc. We write some prompts, we look at outputs, we grade them. And the thing I'm worried about is that as models get more capable, the gap between what the eval measures and what we actually care about widens. A model that's good at looking aligned on a test and a model that is aligned look identical from the outside. So I'd love to see more rigorous work on eval validity, on how you detect when a model is behaving differently under evaluation than in deployment, and on the statistics of making confident claims from relatively small numbers of samples. That feels like infrastructure the whole field needs and nobody's really incentivized to build.

The second is interpretability aimed at a specific question rather than interpretability in general. A lot of mechanistic interpretability has been — and I don't mean this dismissively — exploratory. Let's see what's in there. That's valuable, but I think there's a lot of room for interpretability that's trying to answer a concrete safety-relevant question. Is this model representing something like "I am being tested right now"? Does it have an internal notion of the overseer's beliefs that differs from its own? Can we tell when a model's stated reasoning and its actual computation diverge? Those are hard, but they're the questions that actually matter for whether we can trust these systems, and I think pointing interpretability at them would be enormously useful.

Third — and this one's more theoretical — I'd like to see more work on what you might call the limits of scalable oversight. We spend a lot of effort trying to make oversight work: debate, recursive reward modeling, having AI help humans supervise AI. But there's much less work on characterizing when these approaches fundamentally can't work. What are the properties of a task that make it impossible to verify a solution even with assistance? If we had a clearer theory of that, we'd know where to put our effort and, importantly, where not to deploy these systems yet. I think the theorists have mostly stayed away from this because it's messy, but even partial results would be really clarifying.

Fourth, I'd put more emphasis on understanding generalization of values and intentions. When we train a model to behave well on a distribution of situations, what does it actually learn? Does it learn the thing we meant, or a proxy that happens to coincide on the training distribution? There's been some good empirical work showing surprising generalization — both good and bad — but we don't have much predictive understanding. If someone could build even a rough science of "when does fine-tuning on X generalize to Y," that would make a lot of our safety training much less of a guessing game.

And then one more that's a bit different in flavor: I think there's underinvestment in red-teaming the alignment research agenda itself. Taking the plans that labs — including the one I'm at — have published, and seriously trying to find the holes. Not in a dismissive way, but in the way a good security researcher attacks a protocol. Where are the load-bearing assumptions? What happens if this particular technique fails silently? A lot of this critique happens informally on forums, which is good, but I think there's room for it to be done more rigorously and written up in a way that's actually actionable for the people building these systems.

The common thread, if there is one, is that I think the field is pretty good at generating techniques and pretty weak at knowing whether the techniques work. And the hard part of alignment isn't going to be having ideas — it's going to be having justified confidence before we deploy something we can't take back. So anything that moves us toward being able to make and check claims about model behavior with real rigor, I'd be very excited to see more of.

astra-6.text:
One direction I’d be excited to see more work on is using AI to help us do alignment research. Can we get models to help us find flaws in our proposals, design better experiments, or understand what’s happening inside another model? If we can make that work reliably, it could substantially increase the amount of alignment research we’re able to do.

Another is understanding how to tell whether we’re actually making progress. It’s relatively easy to show that a technique improves a model’s behaviour on some set of examples. It’s much harder to know whether that improvement will hold up when the model is more capable, or operating in circumstances we didn’t anticipate. I’d be excited about evaluations that really probe that gap.

And more broadly, I’d like to see people pursue approaches that challenge our assumptions. There’s a lot of uncertainty here, so having independent researchers try different things—and explain where the approaches we’re pursuing might fail—seems very valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I’d be excited to see more of is work on understanding what’s actually going on inside neural networks. If we train a model to behave in ways that look aligned, can we tell whether it has learned what we intended, or whether it’s using some other strategy that happens to work on our evaluations? Having better tools for answering that would be really valuable.

I’d also like to see more work on evaluating alignment techniques. It’s easy to propose an approach, but much harder to design an experiment that tells you where it breaks and whether the problem will get worse as models become more capable. Can we create settings where a model has an opportunity to deceive its overseer, for example, and then test whether our methods actually catch that?

More broadly, I think it’s healthy to have people pursuing different approaches with different assumptions. We don’t know which parts of the problem will turn out to be hardest, so I wouldn’t want everyone working on the same agenda.
